newsitem.title: TURKEY: Pro-Baghdad Kurdish chief to meet U.S. envoy.
newsitem.headline: Pro-Baghdad Kurdish chief to meet U.S. envoy.

text.p: Kurdish leader Massoud Barzani is to meet a senior U.S. official in Turkey, just days after his fighters took control of northern Iraq with the backing of Baghdad's troops, a Kurdish group said on Tuesday.
The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) said its chief Barzani would hold talks this week with Robert Pelletreau, the U.S. assistant secretary of state for near eastern affairs.
"There will be discussions on the whole new situation in Iraqi Kurdistan," KDP London-based spokesman Dilshad Miran said.
Sources close to the talks told Reuters the session could be held either in Ankara or the town of Silopi near the Iraqi border, as early as Wednesday.
"A meeting has been requested. We are trying to put it together," a diplomatic source said. She did not say who had asked for the meeting.
Barzani's forces conquered most of northern Iraq last week in fighting with a rival militia led by Jalanl Talabani.

The clashes shattered a U.S.-brokered ceasefire and boosted Iraqi President Saddam Hussein in an area that has been out of his control since a Western no-fly zone was imposed over northern Iraq after the 1991 Gulf War.

Barzani's group says it was forced to ask for Baghdad's help to counter Iranian support for the rival group. The KDP complains that Washington did not do enough to help implement a tentative peace deal between the Kurds agreed last year.
"We need some clear answers. Over the years we have been asking the Americans, the State Department, what their policies are on the Kurdish issue," Miran said.
Iraqi troops and tanks helped Barzani capture a key Kurdish city last month, prompting U.S. missile strikes on Iraq.
A new U.S. attack on Iraq appeared uncertain in the face of Baghdad's retreat from confrontation and a dearth of diplomatic support for President Bill Clinton's tough line toward Saddam.
The U.S. nuclear-powered submarine Pittsburgh was passing through the Suez Canal on Tuesday en route to join other American forces in the Gulf.
The United States helped around 2,500 pro-U.S. Kurds flee northern Iraq in fear of Saddam last weekend in an acknowledgement that Washington had lost much of its leverage in the mountainous region.
Baghdad's involvement in the Kurdish infighting has raised questions on the effectiveness of a U.S.-led air force in Turkey set up in 1991 to protect the Kurds from any Iraqi attack.

The Kurdish-held north was opened to traffic and goods from the Arab south of Iraq after a five-year break following Barzani's victory. But Barzani, a veteran of a decades-old guerrilla war for Kurdish autonomy from Baghdad, has not announced any definite political deal with Saddam.
Western diplomats say the Kurdish chieftain might still be open to U.S. calls not to get too close to the Iraqi leader.
The KDP said Barzani would also hold talks with Turkish officials on tightening border security.

Turkey says instability in northern Iraq plays into the hands of its own separatist Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), which maintains bases there, but Ankara has yet to unveil details of a proposed security zone in northern Iraq.
Interior Minister Mehmet Agar told journalists he had discussed U.S. help for a plan to install electronic equipment on the Turkish-Iraq border at a meeting with Pelletreau on Monday.
"It was a very positive meeting on border security and the fight against terorism," Agar told reporters.
